summary: Specifies an optional Quick-Start mechanism where a transport protocol and routers cooperate to determine an allowed initial sending rate, and at times a rate after an idle period. It is designed for several transports but focuses on TCP. This RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a new download starts slow, like carefully testing a pool's water. Quick-Start asks the routers along the way if it is safe to go faster right away.

questions: how to speed up tcp slow start
subtitle: Ask routers if you can send faster at the beginning of a TCP connection.

tldr.problem: TCP begins every connection slowly, probing the network for available bandwidth. For small or moderate transfers, this slow-start phase wastes time even when the path has abundant unused capacity.
tldr.mechanism: Quick-Start adds an optional mechanism where the sender requests a higher initial rate in an IP option, routers along the path approve or deny based on their available bandwidth, and the receiver confirms the approval via a TCP option.
tldr.outcome: If approved by all routers, the connection can start at a much higher sending rate. If any router denies it, normal TCP slow-start applies. Quick-Start is an experimental feature for controlled environments.

facts.label: Rate encoding
facts.value: K * 2^N where K=40,000 bps, N=0-15, yielding 0 to 1.3 Gbps

today: RFC 4782 is an Experimental specification and is not widely deployed. Quick-Start sees some use in controlled networks and data centers but has not achieved significant adoption on the public Internet due to router support and deployment challenges.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Each TCP connection begins by determining the appropriate sending rate through a process called slow-start. The sender starts with a small congestion window (1 to 4 segments) and doubles it each round-trip time as long as no congestion is detected. This approach is conservative and safe, but for transfers over uncongested paths with large bandwidth or long latency, slow-start takes many round-trip times before fully utilizing the available capacity.

For moderate-sized file transfers that complete in just a few round-trip times, the slow-start phase can dominate the total transfer time. Quick-Start addresses this by letting the sender explicitly request a higher initial rate and asking routers to approve it. The request includes a requested rate, routers approve by decrementing a special TTL counter if they have free capacity, and the receiver reports back whether the request was approved.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a download starts at 1 segment and takes log(N) round trips to reach N segments. Quick-Start lets you ask 'Can I start at segment M instead?' If all routers say yes, you do. If anyone says no, you go back to normal slow.

sections.title: How Quick-Start Works
sections.content:
Quick-Start operates by having endpoints and routers work together. The sender puts a Quick-Start Request in an IP header option containing a desired sending rate in bits per second and a special Quick-Start TTL (QS TTL). Each router that understands Quick-Start and approves the request decrements the QS TTL by the same amount it decrements the regular IP TTL.

The receiver calculates the difference between the QS TTL and the regular IP TTL: if they match, all routers decremented both equally, meaning all approved. The receiver reports this TTL difference back to the sender in a TCP option called the Quick-Start Response. A mismatch in TTL differences indicates an unsupporting router, which means the request was implicitly denied. If approved, the sender can send an initial congestion window calculated from the approved rate and the round-trip time, transmitted at a controlled pace. After one round-trip time or upon receiving the first acknowledgement, normal TCP congestion control resumes.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender includes a special TTL counter in the IP header. Routers that like the request subtract from it. If the counter matches what was expected when the reply comes back, everyone approved. If it's different, someone said no.

sections.title: IP and TCP Options
sections.content:
The Quick-Start Request is encoded in an 8-byte IP option containing a 4-bit function code (0000 for a request), a 4-bit rate request field, the QS TTL byte, and a 30-bit nonce with a 2-bit reserved field. The rate request field uses the encoding K * 2^N, where K is 40,000 bps and N is 0 to 15, yielding rates from 0 to 1.3 Gbps in 16 steps.

Routers that approve the request decrement the QS TTL but may reduce the rate request if they cannot support the full rate. They must also modify the QS Nonce field if they reduce the rate. A Report of Approved Rate is a companion IP option (function code 1000) sent after the request is approved, echoing the approved rate and nonce to allow routers to track the flow's bandwidth consumption.

In TCP, the Quick-Start Response option carries the TTL difference, the approved rate, and the nonce. This lets the sender verify that the response matches the request and that routers genuinely approved it.
sections.plainLanguage: The request says 'I want to send at rate N' using 4 bits. Routers shrink N if needed but keep the same password-like number. The reply comes back in a TCP option saying 'we approved this rate.'

sections.title: Connection Establishment and Data Transfer
sections.content:
Quick-Start is typically initiated during TCP's three-way handshake. The client includes a Quick-Start Request in the SYN packet; routers along the forward path process it. The server receives the request, calculates the TTL difference, and if the request appears valid, includes a Quick-Start Response in the SYN/ACK packet along with its own Quick-Start Request for the reverse direction.

The client receives the SYN/ACK, verifies the Quick-Start Response, and if valid, sets its initial congestion window based on the approved rate and measured round-trip time, then sends a Report of Approved Rate in the ACK packet. The server does likewise for its direction. Once the initial Quick-Start window is sent, the connection falls back to normal TCP congestion control.

Quick-Start can also be used in the middle of a connection (e.g., after an idle period) to request a rate increase, provided the requested rate is not less than the current sending rate.
sections.plainLanguage: During the SYN, client asks routers for a faster rate. Routers say yes or no by keeping or changing the counter. Server says 'approved at this rate' in the SYN/ACK. Client and server then send faster for one round trip, then use normal congestion control.

sections.title: Limitations and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
Quick-Start has significant deployment challenges. Many routers and middleboxes drop packets with unknown IP options, so a Quick-Start SYN might be lost entirely, forcing a three-second timeout before retry. Some networks use tunneling or IP-in-IP encapsulation that breaks Quick-Start TTL tracking, potentially causing false positives where the sender incorrectly believes approval when no approval occurred. Multipath routing, where different packets follow different paths, defeats Quick-Start because the TTL difference would not match consistently.

To address these issues, the RFC specifies that Quick-Start is intended for controlled environments where all routers along the path support it and where consistent paths are assured. Tunnels can be configured to zero the Quick-Start option before encapsulation to avoid false positives. Core routers are unlikely to implement Quick-Start because the per-flow bookkeeping and QoS decision complexity do not justify the benefit at the backbone level.
sections.plainLanguage: Many old routers drop packets with unknown options, so the request might vanish and you have to wait and retry. Some networks tunnel things in ways that fool the counter-checking. Quick-Start works best in private, controlled networks, not across the wild Internet.

sections.title: Security and Robustness
sections.content:
Quick-Start's main security mechanism is the QS Nonce, a 30-bit random value that routers must modify (along with the rate) if they reduce the approved rate. This nonce helps prevent receivers from lying about the approved rate, and it prevents collusion between routers because the nonce change would reveal the inconsistency.

However, a misbehaving sender could exceed the approved rate. The RFC recommends that networks deploy traffic policers to enforce the approved rate. A misbehaving receiver could lie about whether a Quick-Start packet was lost, but TCP loss detection (retransmission timers and duplicate ACKs) would eventually reveal this. If a Quick-Start packet is lost, the sender falls back to standard TCP congestion control, which is safe but inefficient. The RFC notes that Quick-Start is not a replacement for standard congestion control but an augmentation of it.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce is a random number that makes it hard to lie about what was approved. If someone cheats by sending too fast, routers can police them. If packets get lost, TCP goes back to slow mode, which is slow but safe.

left.desc: Start with 1-4 segments, double each RTT until congestion detected.

right.desc: Start with a higher window approved by routers, fall back to slow-start if denied.
